message.content:
You are continuing a real, in-production game-catalog verification sweep on the Nxeon hosting platform (a Hostinger-style VPS/game-server host, codebase at /opt/nxeon on this Proxmox primary host, second compute node at 178.63.94.114 called "node-2"). A prior agent (same task lineage) already completed the first 10 of 47 game families and found 9 real bugs (8 shipped to production, all committed to git and documented in docs/DOCUMENTATION.md). Your job is to continue the identical procedure on the 32 remaining families.

## Read this first, in order

1. `/tmp/claude-0/-root/4f329df3-66ee-49c8-a6c5-615ecf189efc/scratchpad/sweep/PROGRESS.md` — the full running log of everything done so far: methodology, exact commands, every bug found with evidence, what's been fixed and how. This is your primary onboarding document. Read it in full before doing anything else.
2. `/tmp/claude-0/-root/4f329df3-66ee-49c8-a6c5-615ecf189efc/scratchpad/sweep/RESULTS.md` — compact summary.
3. The harness scripts in that same directory: `sweep-one.sh` (provision → wait → in-guest verify → external reachability check for one family; does NOT tear down by design), `teardown.sh` (destroy the VM + delete DB rows), `provision.ts`, `wait.sh`, `verify.sh`, `info.ts`, `udpcheck.sh`, `teardown-db.ts`, `apply.ts`, `list-plans.ts`, `status.ts`, `connect.sh`, `rcontest.mjs`. Read each before using it so you understand exactly what it does — don't guess from the filename.
4. `docs/DOCUMENTATION.md` — search for the sections the prior agent wrote (about the RCON exposure fix, the disk-sizing regression, the Rust/Valheim/Terraria fixes, etc.) to understand the documentation style/format you should match for anything new you find and fix.

## IMPORTANT — a real storage-leak incident from this exact sweep, fixed just now, read carefully

After the first 10-family pass, the owner noticed node-2's backup disk (`/tank/backup`, Proxmox storage `vmdata-hdd`) had an orphaned 8.4GB vzdump archive (`vzdump-qemu-108-...vma.zst`) for a VM that no longer existed in Proxmox OR any database — almost certainly left over from testing the platform's backup FEATURE on some earlier sweep test server, where `teardown.sh` destroyed the VM but never touched the backup archive it had itself created (Proxmox deliberately keeps vzdump backups independent of the live VM's disk — that's correct behavior for real customers, but pure waste for a throwaway test VM). This has already been fixed: `teardown.sh` now also runs `find /tank/backup/dump /var/lib/vz/dump -maxdepth 1 -name "vzdump-qemu-$VMID-*" -print -delete` on node-2 as part of every teardown. **You MUST use the updated teardown.sh for every family** (don't hand-roll your own teardown). If you ever manually run `vzdump` yourself for any reason (e.g. testing the backup/restore feature specifically), you are personally responsible for deleting that archive afterward — check `ssh root@178.63.94.114 'ls -la /tank/backup/dump/ /var/lib/vz/dump/'` before and after any backup-feature test to prove nothing was left behind. Before you finish your run (or if you stop early to report), verify one more time that `/tank/backup/dump/` on node-2 is empty (or contains only archives for VMs that still legitimately exist) — this is now a required part of your own final cleanup verification, exactly like checking for leaked VMs and orphaned DB rows.

## The 32 remaining families

sdtd, vrising, enshrouded, factorio, gmod, conan, unturned, theforest, sonsoftheforest, bedrock, dragonwilds, sunkenland, abioticfactor, corekeeper, icarus, arkasa, soulmask, dst, vintagestory, necesse, tf2, l4d2, nightingale, squad, spaceengineers, kf2, barotrauma, sandstorm, mordhau, theisle, stationeers, eco, empyrion

Per the prior agent's notes: watch arkasa/sdtd/conan/icarus specifically for the same advertised-disk-too-small issue already found and partially mitigated (CS2/ARK/Project Zomboid); watch bedrock/conan/vrising for the same root-owned-bind-mount-vs-uid-1000-container issue found in CS2. These are hints to watch for, not assumptions — verify each family independently and don't assume a bug exists just because a cousin family had one.

## What "verify end-to-end" means (same bar as the first 10 families)

For each family: provision for real on node-2, wait for it to actually come up (not just "job says done"), verify reachability from OUTSIDE the box (the actual join port a customer would use, not just SSH), then — this is the part that matters most, per the original owner brief — actually change a real setting through the platform's own config-apply path and confirm it took effect on the live, running game server (not just that the API call returned success). Then tear down completely (VM + DB rows + any backup archives, per the fix above) before moving to the next family. Only `palworld`, `minecraft`, `rust`, `valheim` currently have a real config-apply implementation (`REAL_APPLY_FAMILIES` in worker/game-config.ts) — for every other family, verifying "settings apply" means confirming whether a real apply path exists at all (most won't) and documenting that gap clearly, NOT building a new one from scratch. Building 30+ new real-apply implementations is far outside this task's scope — a sweep verifying what exists and fixing genuine bugs it finds, not a feature-development project. If a family's install is unusually large/slow, budget real wait time for it (the prior agent found some games take much longer than the original 300s timeout assumed — that specific timeout bug is already fixed, but big installs are still just slow in wall-clock terms).

## Standing rules from this session, already proven across the first 10 families — follow them exactly

- Never fabricate or assume a result — every claim needs real evidence (an actual off-box connection, an actual RCON/log read-back, an actual `git log` check).
- Fix real bugs you find with real, minimal, tested commits — don't refactor beyond what's needed, don't add speculative abstractions.
- Every fix: commit to git with a clear message, verify `tsc`/tests still pass at the existing baseline, deploy staging→prod the same way the prior agent did (see PROGRESS.md for the exact deploy commands used), write it up in docs/DOCUMENTATION.md matching the existing style, in the same commit or a paired `docs:` commit like the prior agent's pattern.
- Never touch a real customer's server. Never send a ticket reply. Never rotate a live credential without flagging it first. If you find something that needs an owner/pricing/business decision (like the prior agent's CS2 and catalog-wide-disk-audit findings), document it clearly as "needs owner decision" and move on — do not act on it yourself.
- Tear down every test VM before moving to the next family — never leave two sweep test VMs running concurrently, and never leave one running when you stop/pause your run for any reason.
- If you stop before finishing all 32 families (e.g. hit a natural checkpoint, or want to report interim findings), that's fine — update PROGRESS.md with exactly where you left off (same as the prior agent did), leave the harness in a clean, resumable state, and make sure node-2 has zero leaked VMs/rows/backups at that checkpoint.

## Reporting

When you finish (all 32 families, or you reach a natural stopping point worth reporting), give a report in the exact same shape as the prior agent's: what you did, bugs found and fixed (with commit hashes), anything needing an owner decision, what's left undone, and explicit confirmation of a clean environment (no leaked VMs, no orphaned DB rows, no orphaned backup archives — check all three).

- figma:figma-generate-design: Use this skill alongside figma-use when the task involves translating an application page, view, or multi-section layout into Figma. Triggers: 'write to Figma', 'create in Figma from code', 'push page to Figma', 'take this app/page and build it in Figma', 'create a screen', 'build a landing page in Figma', 'update the Figma screen to match code', 'convert this modal/dialog/drawer/panel to Figma'. This is the preferred workflow skill whenever the user wants to build or update a full page, modal, dialog, drawer, sidebar, panel, or any composed multi-section view in Figma from code or a description. Discovers design system components, variables, and styles from Code Connect files, existing screens, and library search, then imports them and assembles views incrementally section-by-section using design system tokens instead of hardcoded values.
- figma:figma-generate-diagram: MANDATORY prerequisite — load this skill BEFORE every `generate_diagram` tool call. NEVER call `generate_diagram` directly without loading this skill first. Also use when the user asks to create or generate any component in Figma — even a single one — since components require proper variable foundations, variant states, and design token bindings to be production-quality. This skill teaches WHAT to build and in WHAT ORDER — it complements the `figma-use` skill which teaches HOW to call the Plugin API. Both skills should be loaded together.

Good for UI mockups and screen flows, landing pages, marketing and social graphics, and print pieces - posters, flyers, brochures as single-page artboards; memos and reports as one flowing artboard. Use when someone wants a design, mockup, wireframe, UI or screen design, landing page, poster, flyer, brochure, banner, card, one-pager, or any visual layout they would rather tweak by hand than in code. Only for CREATING or re-seeding a canvas; an existing one is edited in its published Artifact.
- dataviz: Use this skill whenever you are about to create ANY chart, graph, plot, dashboard, or data visualization, in ANY output medium — an HTML or React artifact, inline SVG, plotting code in any library (matplotlib, plotly, d3, Recharts, …), an image/PNG you will render and upload, or a chart shared into Slack. 112	### Bug #5 — healthy game servers failed for having a big download (FIXED, shipped `08a16a1`/`8eb4813`)
113	
114	`provision-health.ts` said its 300s timeout was "a principled default … **not an empirically
115	measured figure** … retuned in one place once real timings are observed". This sweep observed them
116	(table below). Every large Steam-based family failed while perfectly healthy.
117	
118	Fix is NOT a bigger number — that would make a genuinely dead server (Terraria's prompt) waste 45
119	min of a customer's time. Instead, once the 300s check fails, provisioning asks the guest whether
120	it is still *working* (`waitOutGameInstall`): root-fs grew, OR the container logged something in
121	the window. Family-agnostic, so no per-image table to drift. `installProgressed()` is pure + unit
122	tested (+5 tests); the probe was verified on a real mid-install ARK guest (`NXP:28275708:2870`).
123	
124	**Safety**: runs only after the existing check already failed (so working families never touch it),
125	any probe error falls back to today's behaviour, hard 45-min ceiling.

128	
129	`[worker] vmid 105, 106, 107, 108, 109, 110, 111, 112 skipped … still holds backup archives` — but
130	**seven of those eight are live customer VMs on the PRIMARY** (`Server.vmid` is unique app-wide) and
131	exactly one (108) actually held an archive. Anyone debugging vmid exhaustion from that line would go
132	hunting seven archives that don't exist. `pickProvisionVmid` now returns
133	`skippedTaken`/`skippedArchived` and both the log and the exhaustion error say which is which (+2 tests).
134	
135	### Measured game-port-open times (for retuning `GAME_PORT_CHECK_TIMEOUT_MS`)
136	
137	`worker/provision-health.ts` says outright that 300s is "a principled default … **not an
138	empirically measured figure** (no real order was placed to time one) — the timeout/interval are
139	named exports so they can be retuned in one place **once real timings are observed**." This sweep is
140	the first time they have been.
141	
142	| family | provision DONE | notes |
143	|---|---|---|
144	| minecraft | 222s | comfortable |
145	| palworld | 285-304s | comfortable |
146	| rust | ~310s | comfortable |
147	| terraria | 451s | ~170s in the game step — over half the budget |
148	| valheim | 456s | ~180s in the game step — over half the budget |
149	| ark | **fails** | >300s; large SteamCMD download |
150	| cs2 | **fails** | ~70GB download, >1h — cannot pass at any realistic timeout |
151	
152	### Mount-ownership watchlist (from CS2's bug)
153	
154	Families whose setup script bind-mounts `/opt/<family>` with no `PUID`/`PGID` and no pre-`chown`:
155	`ark, bedrock, conan, cs2, minecraft, palworld, rust, terraria, valheim, vrising`.
156	
157	That static list over-reports — an image that runs as root, or chowns the mount itself, is fine.
158	Already empirically cleared by this sweep: **minecraft, palworld, rust, valheim** (all verified
159	writing into their mounts). Confirmed broken: **cs2**. Still to be resolved by the sweep as each is
160	provisioned: `ark, bedrock, conan, terraria, vrising`.
161	
162	### Bug #7 — the concurrent disk-sizing change broke Project Zomboid (FIXED, shipped `b13b2ab`/`7e0ca88`)
163	
164	The risk flagged below stopped being hypothetical within hours. `c59d9bc` sized game VMs from the
165	advertised `gamePlan` numbers instead of the linked `basePlan` tier. Right for RAM/cores; **wrong for
166	disk**, where less doesn't mean "runs smaller", it means "cannot install".
167	
168	Live proof on the very next PZ provision:
169	```
170	91.80% /project-zomboid/media/videos/Echocreek.bik
171	Download failed to due to an unhandled exception:
172	  No space left on device : '/project-zomboid/media/videos/FallasLake.bik'
173	/dev/sda1  14G  14G  0  100% /
174	```
175	PZ entry plan ("6 GB / 8 players", $9.00) advertises **15GB**; the install doesn't fit. And it IS a
176	regression, not pre-existing: **a real customer ordered the identical plan 30 minutes before that
177	commit** (`projectzomboid-kc0kcr` 07:39 vs 08:10) and provisioned fine on the linked Pro tier's 80GB.
178	
179	Fix: `Math.max(gamePlan.diskGB, plan.diskGB)`. RAM/cores keep `c59d9bc`'s correction untouched.
180	
181	**Owner decision:** measured install requirements so far — **CS2 66.2 GiB / 58.42 GB prealloc,
182	ARK 22.9 GB, Project Zomboid >15 GB**. Setting advertised disk sizes the games actually fit in is a
183	pricing call.
184	
185	### Cross-cutting risk introduced mid-sweep by a CONCURRENT session (owner should know)
186	
187	At 08:10, while this sweep was running, another session committed `c59d9bc` ("Fix game orders being
188	provisioned to their linked basePlan's full size instead of what was actually sold"). It makes
189	`provision()` size game VMs from `gamePlan` (the advertised numbers) instead of `basePlan`. In
190	principle correct — customers should get what they bought. But measured against the live catalog:
191	
192	**116 of 121 game plans get a SMALLER disk under the new sizing**, often much smaller:
193	
194	```
195	  Abiotic Factor — 6 GB / 4 players     80GB -> 25GB
196	  ARK — 8 GB / 20 slots                 80GB -> 40GB
197	  Bedrock — 1 GB / 5 players            25GB ->  5GB
198	  Conan Exiles — 6 GB / 20 slots        80GB -> 30GB
199	  Dragonwilds — 6 GB / 5 players        80GB -> 25GB
200	  ...
201	```
202	
203	CS2's own gamePlan disks are 40GB/50GB — still far under its 58.42GB preallocation, so CS2 stays
204	impossible either way. But the general question is now live for every family: **is each advertised
205	disk actually big enough for that game's install?** Nobody has checked, and the games with the
206	largest installs (arkasa at 70GB advertised, ark, sdtd, conan, icarus) are exactly where it would
207	bite. From this point on this sweep provisions with the new sizes, so it tests what customers will
208	really get.
209	
210	Note: that commit reached production inside **this sweep's own promote** — the deploy scripts sync
211	to `main`, so a concurrent session's work rides along. Flagging rather than judging; it passed tsc
212	and the test suite alongside my own changes.
213	
214	### Bug #2 — eight families forwarded RCON, not the join port (FIXED, shipped `3be5383`/`c4d378c`)
215	
216	`GAME_PORT` is a health-CHECK map (prefers a TCP port because a TCP connect proves the game bound
217	it). Provisioning reused it as the forward-this-port map. For **rust, ark, projectzomboid, factorio,
218	arkasa, soulmask, squad, kf2** it names an RCON/query/admin port and the join port is a different
219	UDP one — `GAME_PORT`'s own comments always said so.
220	
221	Live proof on a fresh Rust provision: guest listening on BOTH 28015/udp and 28016/tcp; node-2 NAT
222	had exactly two rules (SSH + 28016/tcp); dashboard showed the customer `178.63.94.114:20019` — their
223	**RCON port** — as the address to give players. Same outage as real customer `rust-w75hko`, from
224	scratch.
225	
226	Fix: `joinPortFor()` + `GAME_JOIN_PORT_OVERRIDE` (8 rows, every one sourced from the family's own
227	`docker run -p` mapping), provisioning forwards the join port, `gameForwardFor()` selects it.
228	Verified: raw UDP from another host moved node-2's DNAT counter 0→6 packets AND tcpdump inside the
229	guest saw them reach the container (`eth0 In > 10.20.1.105.28015`, `docker0 Out > 172.17.0.2.28015`).
230	+3 tests.
231	
232	### Bug #3 — SECURITY: game RCON published to the internet with the image default password (FIXED, shipped `196e5c9`/`1e71d69`)
233	
234	Asking what was actually on the forwarded 28016: **Rust's WebSocket RCON answered from off-box and
235	returned a full `serverinfo` dump**, password `docker` (didstopia bakes `+rcon.password docker`;
236	`prisma/catalog.ts` never overrides). Ban/kick/any-convar/wipe control, from the internet, on the
237	port the dashboard was telling customers to hand to players. ark + projectzomboid seed
238	`changeme12` similarly.
239	
240	**Blast radius zero, narrowly** — the only real customer in these families (`rust-w75hko`) predates
241	auto-forwarding and holds only its join port (checked from the DB, no customer server touched). The
242	next order of any of the eight would have been exposed.
243	
244	Fix: retract the check-only forward after the check passes. End state = SSH + join port only.
245	Nothing internal regresses (`lib/game-control.ts` tunnels RCON to 127.0.0.1 over SSH). Verified:
246	rule gone on resync, the RCON that had just answered now unreachable, SSH + join port untouched.
247	
248	**Owner decision still open:** the images ship default admin credentials that survive regardless of
249	forwarding. Per-server generated RCON passwords surfaced in the panel = a feature, needs a product call.
250	
251	### Bug #4 — applyRust wrote a config file this image completely ignores (FIXED, pending verify)
252	
253	Two independent problems, both proven live:
254	1. **No `server.cfg` exists.** Rust ships none; the image creates only `bans.cfg`, `users.cfg`,
255	   `serverauto.cfg`, `relay_cfg.json` in `/opt/rust/server/docker/cfg/`. `remoteLocate` only matches
256	   existing files → every apply soft-failed "Could not locate Rust server.cfg".
257	2. **Fixing the path would not have helped.** Wrote `server.hostname "NXEON SWEEP TEST HOSTNAME"` +
258	   `server.maxplayers 42` into the real cfg dir, restarted, and RCON still reported
259	   `Hostname: Rust Server [DOCKER]`, `MaxPlayers: 500`. `didstopia/rust-server` builds its whole
260	   launch line from `RUST_SERVER_*` env vars (`/app/start.sh`, read directly off the container), and
261	   those win. Same class as Palworld's regenerate-then-lose bug.
262	
263	Fix: rewrote `applyRust` to the container-recreation pattern, and extracted
264	`recreateGameContainer()` + `readContainerEnv()` + `writeEnvFile()` as shared helpers so palworld
265	and rust cannot drift. Env mapping read out of the image's own `start.sh`:
266	`hostname→RUST_SERVER_NAME`, `maxplayers→RUST_SERVER_MAXPLAYERS`, `worldsize→RUST_SERVER_WORLDSIZE`,
267	`seed→RUST_SERVER_SEED`, and `pve` via `RUST_SERVER_STARTUP_ARGUMENTS` (the image's own escape hatch).
268	
269	Verified so far: container recreated `restart=no`, unit active `NRestarts 0`, ports preserved, no
270	stray container, env updated, and the **real running process's argv** now carries
271	`+server.hostname NXEON SWEEP RUST +server.maxplayers 42 +server.pve true +server.worldsize 4000`.
272	
273	### Bug #1 — game-config apply fought systemd for the container (FIXED, shipped)
274	
275	`worker/index.ts`'s `wrapDockerGameService()` turns EVERY family's `docker run -d --name X` setup
276	script into `docker create` + a `<hint>.service` systemd unit (`Restart=always`, `RestartSec=5`) and
277	deliberately strips docker's own `--restart` policy. So systemd — not docker — owns every game
278	container. `applyPalworld` talked to docker directly.
279	
280	- **The revival race the 2026-09-05 fix claimed to close was half-open.** Disabling docker's policy
281	  closes docker's half only. `docker stop` makes the unit's ExecStart (`docker start -a`) exit →
282	  systemd restarts it 5s later. Live journal during an apply:
283	  `05:23:19 Deactivated successfully` → `05:23:24 Scheduled restart job, restart counter is at 1`.
284	  The function had a 5-second budget to finish its rename+recreate.
285	- **Every successful apply re-added `--restart unless-stopped`**, permanently double-supervising the
286	  container — the exact state the provisioning wrapper exists to prevent. Confirmed on the real
287	  container post-apply: `restart=unless-stopped` + still-enabled `palworld.service`.
288	
289	Fix: shared `resolveGameUnit()` (resolves the unit from `controlSpec().serviceHints`), then
290	`systemctl stop` → `docker create` (no `--restart`) → `systemctl start`, plus a real
291	`.State.Running` confirmation before the rollback target is deleted. No unit resolved → old path
292	verbatim. Verified live: 4 settings read back off disk, `restart=no`, `NRestarts: 0`, clean
293	`Stopping → Stopped → Started` journal.
294

1	#!/usr/bin/env bash
2	# Full teardown of one sweep test server: destroy the VM on node-2, then delete
3	# every DB row (the lesson from 2026-09-06's two orphaned-vmid collisions).
4	# Usage: teardown.sh <serverId> <vmid>

11	# any vmid belonging to a VM this sweep did not create.

13	  100|101|102|103|104|9000|9001|9002|9003|9004)

18	ssh -o StrictHostKeyChecking=no -o ConnectTimeout=20 "root@$NODE" \
19	  "qm stop $VMID 2>&1; sleep 4; qm destroy $VMID --purge 1 --destroy-unreferenced-disks 1 2>&1" || true

21	echo "=== confirming it is gone ==="

26	# backup archives independent of the live VM (so destroying a real customer's VM
27	# never silently destroys its disaster-recovery backup too). For a THROWAWAY sweep
28	# test VM that guarantee has no value and pure cost: found an 8.4GB orphaned
29	# archive from an earlier, untracked vzdump on node-2's backup disk (2026-09-06)

31	# vmid on every configured backup-content storage, not just the default one.

1	#!/usr/bin/env bash
2	# Poll a PROVISION job until it reaches DONE or FAILED (or the deadline).
3	# Usage: wait.sh <serverId> [maxSeconds]
4	set -u
5	SW=/tmp/claude-0/-root/4f329df3-66ee-49c8-a6c5-615ecf189efc/scratchpad/sweep
6	SID="$1"
7	MAX="${2:-1800}"
8	cd /opt/nxeon
9	START=$(date +%s)
10	LAST=""
11	until false; do
12	  OUT=$(npx tsx "$SW/status.ts" "$SID" 2>&1)
13	  ST=$(printf '%s' "$OUT" | python3 -c 'import sys,json;d=json.load(sys.stdin);print((d.get("job") or {}).get("status",""))' 2>/dev/null)
14	  STEP=$(printf '%s' "$OUT" | python3 -c 'import sys,json;d=json.load(sys.stdin);print((d.get("server") or {}).get("provisioningStep") or "")' 2>/dev/null)
15	  NOW=$(date +%s); EL=$((NOW-START))
16	  if [ "$ST$STEP" != "$LAST" ]; then
17	    echo "[${EL}s] job=$ST step=$STEP"
18	    LAST="$ST$STEP"
19	  fi
20	  case "$ST" in
21	    DONE|FAILED) echo "FINAL after ${EL}s:"; printf '%s\n' "$OUT"; exit 0 ;;
22	  esac
23	  if [ "$EL" -ge "$MAX" ]; then echo "TIMEOUT after ${EL}s:"; printf '%s\n' "$OUT"; exit 2; fi
24	  sleep 5
25	done

225	 * `GAME_PORT` is a HEALTH-CHECK map. Where an image exposes a TCP port at all it
226	 * prefers that one, because "a TCP handshake is verifiable with a plain connect,
227	 * and the process binding it is proof the game server itself came up" — see its
228	 * own comment. For most families that port is also the join port, so the
229	 * distinction never mattered. For the eight below it is an RCON/query/admin
230	 * port, and `GAME_PORT`'s own inline comments have always said so.
231	 *
232	 * It started mattering the moment provisioning began auto-forwarding "the game's
233	 * own port" for NAT servers using this same map. Found live 2026-09-06 by
234	 * provisioning a real Rust server on node-2: the guest listened correctly on
235	 * 28015/udp (join) and 28016/tcp (RCON), the node's NAT had exactly one game
236	 * rule — 28016/tcp — and the dashboard handed the customer that RCON port as
237	 * their connect address. No player could ever have joined. That is the identical
238	 * outage found on the real paying customer `rust-w75hko` (see
239	 * docs/DOCUMENTATION.md's node migration section), whose root cause was
240	 * previously read as "allocateGameForward was never called for it"; it is called,
241	 * just with the wrong port.
242	 *
243	 * Every entry is sourced from the family's own `docker run -p ...` mapping in
244	 * prisma/catalog.ts / the seed-wave*-games.ts files — the only ports docker
245	 * actually exposes off the container — cross-checked against the join port
246	 * `GAME_PORT`'s own comment already names. Anything NOT listed here joins on its
247	 * `GAME_PORT` entry; use {@link joinPortFor} rather than reading this directly.
248	 */
249	const GAME_JOIN_PORT_OVERRIDE: Partial<Record<GameFamily, { port: number; protocol: "tcp" | "udp" }>> = {
250	  rust: { port: 28015, protocol: "udp" }, // GAME_PORT is 28016/tcp rcon
251	  ark: { port: 7777, protocol: "udp" }, // GAME_PORT is 27020/tcp rcon
252	  projectzomboid: { port: 16261, protocol: "udp" }, // GAME_PORT is 27015/tcp rcon
253	  factorio: { port: 34197, protocol: "udp" }, // GAME_PORT is 27015/tcp rcon
254	  arkasa: { port: 7777, protocol: "udp" }, // GAME_PORT is 27020/tcp rcon
255	  soulmask: { port: 8777, protocol: "udp" }, // GAME_PORT is 18888/tcp telnet admin
256	  squad: { port: 7787, protocol: "udp" }, // GAME_PORT is 21114/tcp rcon
257	  kf2: { port: 7777, protocol: "udp" }, // GAME_PORT is 8080/tcp webadmin
258	};

264	 * the eight in `GAME_JOIN_PORT_OVERRIDE`.
265	 */

content.content:
## Eight game families forwarded RCON instead of the port players join on (2026-09-06)

Third finding of the whole-catalog integrity sweep, and the most customer-visible one so far. A
fresh Rust provision on node-2 came up perfectly healthy and was still completely unjoinable.

**`lib/games.ts`'s `GAME_PORT` is a health-CHECK map, and provisioning was reusing it as a
forward-this-port map.** Those answer different questions. `GAME_PORT` deliberately prefers a TCP
port wherever an image exposes one, because — in its own words — "a TCP handshake is verifiable with
a plain connect, and the process binding it is proof the game server itself came up, which is
exactly the class of bug this check exists to catch — even though it isn't the port the player's
game client uses to join". For 39 families that port is also the join port and the distinction never
mattered. For **eight** it is an RCON/query/admin port, and `GAME_PORT`'s own inline comments have
always said so:

| family | `GAME_PORT` (health check) | port players actually join on |
|---|---|---|
| rust | 28016/tcp (rcon) | **28015/udp** |
| ark | 27020/tcp (rcon) | **7777/udp** |
| projectzomboid | 27015/tcp (rcon) | **16261/udp** |
| factorio | 27015/tcp (rcon) | **34197/udp** |
| arkasa | 27020/tcp (rcon) | **7777/udp** |
| soulmask | 18888/tcp (telnet admin) | **8777/udp** |
| squad | 21114/tcp (rcon) | **7787/udp** |
| kf2 | 8080/tcp (webadmin) | **7777/udp** |

It started mattering when provisioning began auto-forwarding "the game's own port" for NAT servers
off that same map. Confirmed live on a real fresh Rust server, not inferred: the guest was listening
correctly on **both** 28015/udp and 28016/tcp; node-2's NAT chain held exactly two rules for it —
SSH, and 28016/tcp; and `app/dashboard/servers/[id]/page.tsx`'s `gameForwardFor()` (which also keyed
on `GAME_PORT`) handed the customer `178.63.94.114:20019` — **their RCON port** — as the address to
give their players. Every NAT game server of those eight families ever provisioned was unjoinable
from the moment it was handed over, and the connect address shown in the dashboard was wrong.

This is the same outage previously found on the real paying customer **`rust-w75hko`** during the
node-2 migration (see the migration section above), whose root cause was read at the time as
"`allocateGameForward()` evidently never got called for it". It does get called — with the wrong
port. The earlier diagnosis fixed that one server by hand; this fixes the cause.

**Fix**, in three parts:
- `lib/games.ts` gains `GAME_JOIN_PORT_OVERRIDE` (exactly the eight rows above) and
  `joinPortFor(family)`, which returns `GAME_PORT`'s entry for everyone else. Every override is
  sourced from that family's own `docker run -p ...` mapping in `prisma/catalog.ts` /
  `seed-wave*-games.ts` — the only ports docker actually exposes off the container — cross-checked
  against the join port `GAME_PORT`'s comment already named. No new research, no guessing.
- `worker/index.ts` allocates a second forward for the join port whenever it differs, for NAT
  servers on any node. **Additive on purpose**: the health-check forward stays, because a
  non-primary node's game-port check runs *through* it (2026-09-06's earlier fix) and removing it
  would break the retry path. Best-effort, like the forward beside it — never fails a provision.
- `gameForwardFor()` selects the join forward first, falling back to the check port and then to any
  forward, so pre-existing servers still show something rather than nothing.

**Verified end-to-end on the real Rust server**, the same way the migration runbook demands for UDP:
allocated the join forward, ran `syncPortForwards()`, then sent raw UDP from a genuinely different
host and confirmed BOTH that node-2's DNAT counter moved (0 → 6 packets / 312 bytes) AND that
`tcpdump` inside the guest saw the packets land — `eth0 In IP …51.79.162.96 > 10.20.1.105.28015`
followed by `docker0 Out … > 172.17.0.2.28015`, i.e. all the way into the container, not merely as
far as the host.

### …and the admin port it forwarded had the image's default password (same day, fixed)

Following the above straight into "so what IS on 28016, then": **Rust's WebSocket RCON answered a
connection from off-box and returned a full `serverinfo` dump**, on a sweep test VM, using the
password `docker`. `didstopia/rust-server` bakes `+rcon.password docker` into its launch line from
`RUST_RCON_PASSWORD`, and `prisma/catalog.ts`'s Rust setup script never overrides it. So the
provisioning path was publishing an unauthenticated-in-practice admin channel — ban/kick any player,
set any convar, wipe the map — to the internet, on a port the dashboard was simultaneously telling
the customer to hand out to their players.

The same shape applies to the other seven: their `GAME_PORT` is an admin port too, and several of
their images ship equally well-known defaults (`ark` and `projectzomboid` both seed
`ADMIN_PASSWORD=changeme12`/`RCON_PASSWORD=changeme12` in `prisma/seed-wave1-games.ts`).

**Blast radius was zero, narrowly.** The only real customer in any of the eight is `rust-w75hko`,
created 2026-08-28 — before auto-forwarding existed — and it holds exactly one forward,
`28015/udp` (its join port, added by hand during the node-2 migration). Checked from the DB alone,
without touching the customer's server. **The next order of any of those eight families would have
been exposed**, which is what makes this worth fixing now rather than filing.

**Fix:** provisioning now *retracts* the check-only forward once the check has served its purpose.
A non-primary node still has to publish `game.port` to check through it at all — that is the only
path that exists there — but as soon as the check passes and the join forward is in place, the
admin forward is deleted and the NAT re-synced. The end state is exactly SSH + the join port.
Nothing internal regresses: the platform's own RCON never used the public forward, it tunnels to
`127.0.0.1:<port>` over SSH (`lib/game-control.ts`). A customer who genuinely wants remote RCON can
still add the forward from the dashboard — deliberately, and knowing what it is.

Verified live on the same Rust VM: forward retracted, NAT rule gone (`-1` on the resync), the
WebSocket RCON that had just answered now unreachable, SSH and `28015/udp` untouched.

**Still an owner decision, deliberately not done here:** these images ship *default* admin
credentials that survive into a customer's running server regardless of whether the port is
published — a customer who adds their own RCON forward re-exposes `docker`/`changeme12`. Generating
a per-server RCON password at provision time and surfacing it in the panel is a feature, not a bug
fix, and it needs a product call on where that credential lives.

This confirms Conan Exiles hits the same CS2 mount-ownership bug: the host directories are root-owned with 0755 permissions, but the container runs as uid 7100, so it can't write to them, and Wine explicitly refuses to proceed as a result.

The 5.2GB the customer has downloaded actually lives in the container's writable layer, not the bind mounts, which are still empty (4.0K). That's a serious problem — any container recreation (which happens during config changes or image updates) will permanently destroy the save data, and the platform's own File Manager and backups see an empty directory since they're targeting mounts the game never actually wrote to. The fix is the same one other families already use: pre-chown the bind mount to the container's uid during setup.

For conan specifically, I need to create `/opt/conan/game` and `/opt/conan/config` and chown them recursively to uid 7100 before the container runs — I confirmed 7100 is the correct uid by running `id conanexiles` inside the live container. I also notice the current script doesn't even `mkdir -p` the directories, letting Docker auto-create them as root, which is part of the problem. Before I finalize the fix I want to actually test it live — apply the chown, recreate the container, and confirm the install lands in `/opt/conan/game` — but I need to be careful since the provisioning job is still mid-install, so restarting the container now could break that job.

Actually, restarting won't hurt since proving the fix is the goal, but the better approach is to let the current provisioning run finish first to record the baseline behavior — likely it'll succeed but silently write data to the wrong (ephemeral) location, which is itself worth documenting. Then, once that's done, I'll stop the unit, chown the mount directories to 7100, recreate the container with the same arguments, and verify the install correctly lands in `/opt/conan/game` before moving on to fixing `prisma/catalog.ts` and the live script.

While that runs in the background, I should also check whether other game families share this same non-root-user-plus-root-owned-mount problem — probably best verified empirically per family like I'm already doing, though I want to note that titles like `theforest`/`sonsoftheforest` using PUID/PGID likely chown their mounts internally at container startup before dropping privileges, whereas Enshrouded's handling may differ.

Confirmed: Conan is stuck in an infinite reinstall loop. Since `/conanexiles` isn't owned by the right uid, Wine can't initialize and reports the game as not installed, so it re-downloads the full 5.3GB game into the writable layer, then fails at the `ln` step because the expected path doesn't exist, causing the container to restart and repeat the cycle.

I'm also noticing something important: the root filesystem is climbing toward 17GB and will eventually fill the disk if this keeps looping. More critically, I'm realizing docker-proxy binds the host port as soon as the container is created — meaning a TCP health check against port 7777 could report success even though the actual game process inside never started, which would make port-based health checks fundamentally unreliable for this kind of dead server.

But wait, I need to reconsider: with `-p`, Docker actually routes external traffic through an iptables DNAT rule to the container's IP directly, not through docker-proxy — docker-proxy mainly handles localhost/hairpin traffic. So if nothing's listening inside the container, an external connection gets a RST and fails properly, which explains why Terraria's health check correctly caught the failure.

The install-progress probe likely sees the root fs still growing since it's stuck re-downloading, so it'll keep reporting "still installing" — the 45-minute hard ceiling is what actually saves us here. I'll let this run to see the real customer-facing outcome: started 12:05, quick check fails ~12:12, then ceiling hits ~12:57, so roughly 50 minutes to FAILED.

While that plays out, I'm drafting the actual fix — pre-creating and chowning the bind-mount directories to the container's uid before the docker run so permissions are correct from the start.

This matches the existing convention across the catalog where other games do the same chown pattern with their respective uids. I need to apply the fix both in the seed source file and directly on the live OsTemplate row, following the same pattern used for the Terraria fix — and I should double check whether the catalog file also references conan somewhere I missed.

These three templates were all created together, so I need to grep catalog.ts to confirm which file actually seeds them before patching. Before making the fix, I should verify it works live: stop the conan systemd unit, chown the directory, then recreate the container to confirm the install lands properly in /opt/conan/game — I'll need to be careful since the wrapDockerGameService-created unit will try to restart the container once I stop it.

Actually the simpler approach is to just stop the unit, chown -R 7100:7100 /opt/conan, and restart it, since the unit reuses the existing container rather than recreating it. But I'm now uncertain where the game actually gets installed inside the container — the writable layer already holds 5.2GB in /home/conanexiles, so I need to figure out whether /conanexiles is the real install target the entrypoint checks against.

The cleanest test is to stop the unit, chown the mounts, remove the existing container, and rerun the original docker run command fresh — that mirrors exactly what a corrected setup script would do, forcing a full 5.3GB redownload but giving a clean verification that /opt/conan/game/ConanSandbox exists and the server actually starts.

## Conan Exiles could never be provisioned either — root-owned bind mounts, then a dead server binary (2026-09-06)

Second family of the whole-catalog integrity sweep found 100% unprovisionable, and the first
confirmation that CS2's bind-mount bug is a *class*, not a one-off. Reproduced on a real provision on
node-2, not inferred.

### Blocker 1 — the container cannot write its own bind mounts (FIXED)

`prisma/seed-wave7-games.ts`'s Conan setup script mounted `-v /opt/conan/game:/conanexiles -v
/opt/conan/config:/conanexiles_config` **without creating or chowning either directory first**, so
docker auto-created both as `root:root 0755`. `melle2/conanexiles-ds` runs as `uid=7100(conanexiles)`.
Straight off the running container:

```
wine: '/conanexiles' is not owned by you, refusing to create a configuration directory there
Game not installed.
Start game download...
...
Game download done.
Link config dir /conanexiles/ConanSandbox/nxeon
ln: failed to create symbolic link '/conanexiles/ConanSandbox/nxeon': No such file or directory
```

Then the entrypoint exits, systemd restarts it 5s later, and it does the whole thing again.
Measured on the live VM after ~20 minutes: **`NRestarts=38`**, both bind mounts still `4.0K`, root
filesystem at 17 GB, `docker ps -s` showing a **5.53 GB writable layer** — i.e. every loop was
re-pulling the 5.3 GB game into the container's own layer, where a single `docker rm` would delete it.
The game port never bound, so the provision failed after all three attempts:

```
game port 7777/tcp never opened on 178.63.94.114:20021 after ~306s ... The install stopped making
progress (3 consecutive minutes with no disk growth and no container output, at 17700 MB used)
```

**Fix:** `mkdir -p /opt/conan/game /opt/conan/config && chown -R 7100:7100 /opt/conan` ahead of the
`docker run`, in `prisma/seed-wave7-games.ts` and in the live `OsTemplate` row (same two-place fix as
Terraria's — the seed file is the source of truth, the row is what provisioning actually reads). This
is the pattern the catalog's other non-root families already use: factorio `chown 845:845`,
sunkenland `chown -R 7000:7000`, theisle `chown -R 1000:1000`.

**Verified live on the same VM** by applying exactly what the fixed script does — stop the unit,
`chown -R 7100:7100 /opt/conan`, recreate the container — and watching the behaviour invert:
`wine: created the configuration directory '/conanexiles/.wine'` (was "refusing to create"),
`Success! App '443030' fully installed.`, `/opt/conan/game` **6.2 GB** (was 4.0K), the config symlink
`ConanSandbox/nxeon -> /conanexiles_config` created without error, and `NRestarts=0` (was 38).

### Blocker 2 — the server binary itself never starts (OWNER DECISION, not fixed)

With the mount bug fixed and the game fully installed *into the mount*, `ConanSandboxServer.exe`
launches under Wine and then does nothing at all. Across two full boots and 35+ minutes:

- the process is alive (`Z:\\conanexiles\\ConanSandboxServer.exe --userdir=nxeon ... -server -log`)
- it has burned **7 CPU ticks total** — `utime stime` = `2 5`, unchanged over a 45-second sample
- it holds 459 MB and 0.00% CPU, on a box with 5.2 GB free and no OOM kills
- `/proc/net/udp` and `/proc/net/tcp` inside the container are **empty** — nothing bound
- nothing is ever written to `/conanexiles_config` (`Saved/Logs/ConanSandbox.log` never appears —
  the image's own `tail` of it fails forever), and `find` turns up no game log anywhere on the box

A second boot, which skips the download entirely, behaves identically. So the mount fix is necessary
and correct — it is a strict improvement, and the customer's install and saves now live in the
persistent mount instead of a disposable container layer — but it is **not sufficient**:
`melle2/conanexiles-ds:latest` does not produce a working Conan Exiles server on this platform.

**This needs the owner**, exactly like CS2's: Conan Exiles is on sale at $14.99/$24.99/$39.99 and
cannot currently be delivered at any tier. Resolving it means sourcing and validating a different
dedicated-server image (or a native, non-Wine install path), which is a catalog/product decision with
real research behind it — not a bug fix. Until then every Conan order will fail provisioning after
~30 minutes of trying.
"""

#!/bin/bash
# Deploy a ref (default: main from /opt/nxeon) to the staging environment.
# Usage: ./scripts/deploy-staging.sh [git-ref]
set -euo pipefail
REF="${1:-main}"
cd /opt/nxeon-staging

echo "==> Syncing staging to $REF"
git fetch origin
git reset --hard "origin/$REF"

echo "==> Installing dependencies"
npm install --no-audit --no-fund 2>&1 | tail -1

echo "==> Applying database schema"
npx prisma db push --accept-data-loss 2>&1 | tail -2
npm run db:seed 2>&1 | tail -2 || true

echo "==> Building"
npm run build 2>&1 | tail -4

# Web runs as the unprivileged 'nxeon' user. Only .next needs to be writable by
# it (Next cache); the rest stays root-owned and world-readable, and systemd
# injects .env as root. Do NOT chown the whole tree (breaks root git on .git).
echo "==> Fixing .next ownership for non-root web"
chown -R nxeon:nxeon /opt/nxeon-staging/.next 2>/dev/null || true
chmod 600 /opt/nxeon-staging/.env 2>/dev/null || true

echo "==> Restarting staging services"
systemctl restart nxeon-staging-web nxeon-staging-worker
sleep 5
systemctl is-active nxeon-staging-web nxeon-staging-worker
CODE=$(curl -s -o /dev/null -w "%{http_code}" http://127.0.0.1:8080/)
echo "==> Staging responds: HTTP $CODE (http://$(grep ^PUBLIC_IP .env | cut -d= -f2):8080)"
[ "$CODE" = "200" ] || { echo "STAGING UNHEALTHY"; exit 1; }
echo "==> Staging deploy complete"
=== PROMOTE ===
#!/bin/bash
# Promote the currently deployed staging commit to production.
# Verifies staging is healthy, fast-forwards nothing (prod working tree IS the repo),
# then rebuilds + restarts production services.
set -euo pipefail

STG_COMMIT=$(git -C /opt/nxeon-staging rev-parse HEAD)
PROD_COMMIT=$(git -C /opt/nxeon rev-parse HEAD)

echo "==> Staging is at:    $STG_COMMIT"
echo "==> Production is at: $PROD_COMMIT"

if ! systemctl is-active -q nxeon-staging-web; then
  echo "Refusing to promote: staging web service is not running." >&2
  exit 1
fi
CODE=$(curl -s -o /dev/null -w "%{http_code}" http://127.0.0.1:8080/)
if [ "$CODE" != "200" ]; then
  echo "Refusing to promote: staging returns HTTP $CODE." >&2
  exit 1
fi

if [ "$STG_COMMIT" != "$PROD_COMMIT" ]; then
  echo "Note: production tree is at a different commit than staging."

# column, silently breaking the FIRST thing that queried it post-deploy
# (found live 2026-09-02: worker/billing.ts's sweeps started throwing
# "column does not exist" immediately after a routine promote — no staging
# failure gave any warning, since staging's own db push had already

# client, so this replaces the old generate-only step rather than adding a
# second one. Schema changes are rare enough that this always running
# unconditionally costs nothing when there's nothing new to push.
echo "==> Applying database schema"
npx prisma db push --accept-data-loss --schema=/opt/nxeon/prisma/schema.prisma 2>&1 | tail -4
echo "==> Building production"
npm run build 2>&1 | tail -4
# Guard: never restart into an incomplete/failed build. A valid production build
# always writes .next/BUILD_ID; if it's missing the build failed mid-way and the
# old in-memory process is still serving — abort rather than kill it.
if [ ! -s /opt/nxeon/.next/BUILD_ID ]; then
  echo "BUILD FAILED: .next/BUILD_ID missing — NOT restarting (old process left serving)." >&2
  exit 1
fi
# Web runs as the unprivileged 'nxeon' user. .next needs to be writable by it
# (Next cache); the rest stays root-owned and world-readable. .env is the one
# exception: systemd's EnvironmentFile= reads it as root (PID 1, pre-privilege
# drop) so the app's process env is fine either way, but Prisma's generated
# client ALSO opens .env directly at Client instantiation to resolve its own
# env() directives — that read happens as the actual 'nxeon' process user, so
# a root-owned .env throws EACCES there on every cold start (harmless once
# systemd's injected vars are already in process.env, but noisy, and a prior
# root-run edit to this file silently reverted the ownership fix below once
# already — confirmed live 2026-09-02). Keep .env nxeon-owned, not world- or
# group-readable. Do NOT chown the whole tree (breaks root git on .git).
echo "==> Fixing .next/.env ownership for non-root web"
chown -R nxeon:nxeon /opt/nxeon/.next 2>/dev/null || true
chown nxeon:nxeon /opt/nxeon/.env 2>/dev/null || true
chmod 600 /opt/nxeon/.env 2>/dev/null || true
echo "==> Restarting production web"
systemctl restart nxeon-web

# Drain in-flight provisions before bouncing the worker. Restarting the worker
# mid-provision used to interrupt a live VM build and (with a non-idempotent retry)
# strand the server in ERROR. The start step is now idempotent so this is
# belt-and-suspenders, but avoiding the interruption entirely is cleaner. Bounded
# wait (max ~4 min) so a deploy can never hang forever.
DBURL=$(grep -E '^DATABASE_URL=' /opt/nxeon/.env | head -1 | cut -d= -f2- | tr -d '"')
if [ -n "$DBURL" ] && command -v psql >/dev/null 2>&1; then
  for _ in $(seq 1 24); do
    ACTIVE=$(psql "$DBURL" -tAc "SELECT count(*) FROM \"Job\" WHERE status='RUNNING' AND type='PROVISION';" 2>/dev/null | tr -d '[:space:]')
    [ "${ACTIVE:-0}" = "0" ] && break
    echo "==> Waiting for ${ACTIVE} in-flight provision(s) to finish before restarting worker…"
    sleep 10
  done
fi

echo "==> Restarting production worker"
systemctl restart nxeon-worker
sleep 5
systemctl is-active nxeon-web nxeon-worker
CODE=$(curl -s -o /dev/null -w "%{http_code}" http://127.0.0.1/)
echo "==> Production responds: HTTP $CODE"
[ "$CODE" = "200" ] || { echo "PRODUCTION UNHEALTHY — check journalctl -u nxeon-web"; exit 1; }
